desc:
You have a board with 2 rows and n columns. You may cover it completely, without overlap, using two kinds of tiles: the domino, a 2×1 rectangle that may be placed horizontally or vertically, and the L-tromino, which covers three cells of a 2×2 block and may be rotated in any of its 4 ways. Every cell must be covered and tiles may not stick out of the board.

Two tilings are different if some pair of adjacent cells is covered by the same tile in one tiling but not in the other. Return the number of tilings modulo 1,000,000,007.

Example: n = 3 gives 5 tilings, n = 4 gives 11.
hints: Draw the first column of a finished tiling. Which tiles can cover its cells?
A vertical domino closes one column (f(n-1)); two horizontal dominoes close two columns (f(n-2)). What about the trominoes? A tromino leaves one cell sticking out, which forces a partner tile.

Every tromino 'bump' must be filled by a matching tromino or by a chain of horizontal dominoes ending in a tromino. These mirror-image shapes give f(n) = 2 · f(n-1) + f(n-3), with f(0) = 1, f(1) = 1, f(2) = 2.
editorial: Let f(n) be the number of tilings of a 2×n board. Look at the leftmost column. A vertical domino covers it and leaves a 2×(n-1) board: f(n-1) ways. Two horizontal dominoes stacked cover two columns: f(n-2) ways. If a tromino covers one of the two left cells, a cell in the next column is also covered, and the board's boundary becomes uneven (a 'staircase' edge). That ragged edge can only be closed by a tromino in the mirrored orientation, or by a run of horizontal dominoes on one row followed by a closing tromino; either way it eventually returns to a flat edge after k ≥ 3 columns, in exactly 2 ways for each k (one for the top-first and one for the bottom-first shape).

This gives f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2) + 2 · (f(n-3) + f(n-4) + ... + f(0)). Subtracting the same equation for n-1 telescopes the sum and leaves f(n) = 2 · f(n-1) + f(n-3), with f(0) = 1, f(1) = 1, f(2) = 2 (check: f(3) = 2·2 + 1 = 5, f(4) = 2·5 + 1 = 11). Three rolling variables and the usual modulo reduction give O(n) time and O(1) space.
